summary: Defines the format of IPv6 global unicast addresses. It obsoletes RFC 2374 and makes the Top Level Aggregator and Next Level Aggregator structure that RFC described historic. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo retires an earlier plan for dividing up global IPv6 addresses. It describes the general address parts as a routing prefix, a subnet ID and an interface ID.

subtitle: The global unicast address layout after the IPv6 TLA/NLA scheme was retired.

tldr.problem: RFC 2374's TLA and NLA allocation structure was no longer considered the right approach for IPv6 address allocation.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3587 makes RFC 2374 historic and describes global unicast addresses as a routing prefix, subnet ID and interface ID.
tldr.outcome: The Regional Internet Registries define a coordinated allocation policy. RFC 3587 is Informational and obsoletes RFC 2374.

today: RFC 3587 is Informational and has no later obsoleting or updating RFC listed in the unit metadata. It obsoletes RFC 2374 and makes the TLA/NLA structure Historic.

sections.title: Retiring the TLA/NLA Structure
sections.content:
RFC 2374 defined an IPv6 address allocation structure with Top Level Aggregator (TLA) and Next Level Aggregator (NLA) fields. RFC 3587 replaces that document and makes both it and the TLA/NLA structure Historic.

The RFC says the scheme was replaced by a coordinated address allocation policy defined by the Regional Internet Registries (RIRs). It cites technical concerns and the policy questions involved in managing address space and routing table size.
sections.plainLanguage: The earlier TLA/NLA address plan is retired. Regional Internet Registries define the coordinated allocation policy described here.

sections.title: Parts of a Global Unicast Address
sections.content:
The general format contains a global routing prefix, a subnet ID and an interface ID. The routing prefix identifies a site, the subnet ID identifies a subnet within that site, and the interface ID follows the IPv6 addressing architecture. The prefix is intended to be structured hierarchically by RIRs and Internet Service Providers, while site administrators structure subnet IDs.

The RFC describes an example using the 2000::/3 prefix: 3 bits for the format prefix, a 45-bit global routing prefix, a 16-bit subnet ID and a 64-bit interface ID. It says implementations should not assume that 2000::/3 will always be the only special allocation. The old SLA field remains in function under the name subnet ID.
sections.plainLanguage: The address has a part for the site, a part for a subnet within it and a part for an interface. The memo's example divides these parts under the 2000::/3 prefix.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC states that IPv6 addressing documents do not have a direct impact on Internet infrastructure security. It does not define additional security mechanisms.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo says that defining IPv6 address formats has no direct effect on Internet infrastructure security.

fields.name: Format prefix
fields.desc: The binary value shown in the example.

fields.name: Subnet ID
fields.desc: Identifies a subnet within the site.

fields.name: Interface ID
fields.desc: Uses Modified EUI-64 format as described in the architecture.
